doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Stravinsky, Ravel, Bartok and Bloch listening; Israel
summary: His collection of recordings, Schelomo, and Carisi's Israel from Birth of the Cool.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: And will always be. I began to listen to Stravinsky’s other works. Then I became aware of Ravel and Bartok and became a real addict of these persons in particular: Stravinsky, Ravel, Bartok, Prokofiev, Richard Strauss, people of that era. I must have five different recordings of Le Sacre [Le Sacre du Printemps by Igor Stravinsky]. I must have five different recorded versions of [Johnson sings the opening measures of the Firebird Suite by Stravinsky].
No, that’s Bartok. Concerto for Orchestra.
The Firebird Suite. I may have five or six different recordings of Ravel’s Daphnis and Chloe and one of my favorite works, a cello scenario, Ernest Bloch's Schelomo.
Schelomo. Right. Wonderful. Tear you heart out.
[It will] tear you heart out, just tear your heart out. That opening cello note will tear your heart out.
That sounds almost like spirituals. It's so powerful.
Johnny Carisi also wrote one of the pieces on that Birth of the Cool album, his piece Israel, which may be the strongest piece of all those pieces.
That's very good. It’s a candidate, right, and it's a strong candidate.
It's held up, when you play it now.
It has stood the test of time. Right. Right. So that was my introduction to classical music.
